Prevalence and Predictors of the Short-Term Trajectory of Anxiety and Depression in the First Year After a Cancer Diagnosis: A Population-Based Longitudinal Study

Allison W. Boyes, Afaf Girgis, Catherine A. D’Este, Alison C. Zucca, Christophe Lecathelinais, and Mariko L. Carey

A B S T R A C T

Purpose Few studies have examined psychological adjustment for cancer survivors in late treatment and early survivorship stages. Our study investigated the prevalence and short-term trajectories of anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety-depression among adult cancer survivors, and identiﬁed the individual, disease, health behavior, psychological, and social predictors of chronic and late psychological morbidity.

Methods A heterogeneous sample of adult cancer survivors was recruited from two state-based cancer registries. A total of 1,154 survivors completed self-report questionnaires at 6 (Time 1) and 12 months (Time 2) postdiagnosis. Anxiety and depression were assessed by the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale with cases identiﬁed by a subscale cutoff score  8. Logistic regression analyses identiﬁed Time 1 characteristics associated with anxiety and/or depression at Time 2.

Results The point prevalence of anxiety (Time 1, 22%; Time 2, 21%), depression (13% at both timepoints) and comorbid anxiety-depression (9% at both timepoints) was similar at 6 and 12 months postdiagnosis. The most prevalent Time 1 to Time 2 trajectory was noncase for anxiety (70%), depression (82%), and comorbid anxiety-depression (87%). While psychological morbidity at Time 1 was the strongest predictor of psychological morbidity at Time 2, being diagnosed with lung cancer and health risk behaviors (smoking, insufﬁcient physical activity) were also strong predictors.

Conclusion Targeted psychological screening of vulnerable survivors and early intervention may prevent the onset and/or reduce the severity of psychological morbidity in early survivorship. Trials of risk reduction interventions targeting psychological functioning and health risk behaviors seem warranted.

J Clin Oncol 31:2724-2729. © 2013 by American Society of Clinical Oncology

INTRODUCTION

With the number of individuals living with a history of cancer expected to triple from 25 million in 2008 to 75 million in 2030,1 attention has turned to how to best maximize the wellbeing of the growing population of cancer survivors. Mental health problems including anxiety and depression often co-occur with cancer and can have an impact on its management.2,3

Bonnano et al4 identiﬁed four patterns of adjustment to traumatic life events: resilience, recovery to normal after high levels of distress, persistent distress, and delayed distress. Henselmans et al5 found that most breast cancer survivors

within the ﬁrst year postdiagnosis experienced no psychological distress (36%) or recovered to normal after completion of active treatment (33%). Small percentages of survivors became distressed soon after active treatment ended (15%) or experienced persistent distress (15%). Understanding the factors that inﬂuence trajectories of psychological adjustment may enable early intervention with survivors at risk of persistent or delayed psychological morbidity. The few previous studies5-10 examining the courseofpsychologicalmorbidityinearlysurvivorship have mostly been conducted with breast cancer survivors and relied on convenience samples drawn from a few treatment centers. To inform the care of the wider

units.text:
Trajectory of Anxiety and Depression in Early Survivorship

populationofsurvivors,callshavebeenmadeforlarge-scalelongitudinal studies with diverse samples.3,11-14

Overcoming limitations of previous research, our study examined the short-term course of anxiety and depression among a large population-based heterogeneous sample of survivors. The speciﬁc aims were to identify the point prevalence of caseness for anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety-depression among adult cancer survivors at 6 and 12 months postdiagnosis; to examine the course of survivors’ anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety-depression levels over the ﬁrst year after diagnosis to identify the proportions of survivors who were noncases, resolved cases, late cases, and chronic cases; and to identify the factors at 6 months postdiagnosis that predicted caseness for anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety-depression at 1 year postdiagnosis.

METHODS

This article is based on data collected at 6 months (Time 1) and 12 months (Time 2) postdiagnosis from survivors participating in the Cancer Sur-vival Study.15-18

Participants and Procedures The sample was recruited from the two largest state-based cancer registries in Australia.15 Sample quotas were set for each registry; one sampled cases proportional to cancer incidence rates and the other sampled consecutive cases until the quota was achieved. Eligible survivors were diagnosed in the previous 6 months with their ﬁrst primary cancer (localized or metastatic) and had one of the top eight incident cancer types in Australia (prostate, colorectal, female breast, lung, melanoma, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, leukemia, or head and neck cancer). Eligible survivors were between 18 and 80 years old and living in the states of New South Wales or Victoria at diagnosis; they were considered by their physician to be aware of their diagnosis, physically and mentally capable of participating in the study, and sufﬁciently proﬁcient in English to complete questionnaires; and they were alive. The sample was restricted to the eight most incident cancers because of registry constraints in the number of cancer types for which rapid case ascertainment procedures could be implemented. Eligible survivors who agreed the registries could pass their contact details on to the researchers received questionnaires to complete at approximately 6 and 12 months postdiagnosis. Participants were cross-checked against the National Death Index to avoid contacting those individuals who had died between time points. Nonresponders received one reminder questionnaire and one reminder phone call 3 weeks apart. Return of a completed questionnaire indicated voluntary consent to participate. The study was ap-proved by the relevant ethics committees.

Measures Data were collected from self-administered questionnaires and cancer registry records. Anxiety and depression were measured by the 14-item Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale (HADS), which includes two subscales: anxiety (HADS-A) and depression (HADS-D).19 A score from 0 to 21 is calculated for each subscale with a higher score indicating a higher level of anxiety or depression. While acknowledging the current debate about the optimal scoring method and cut point to use,20,21 the established subscale cutoff score of  8 was used to identify cases of HADS-A and cases of HADS-D.19,22 Cases of both HADS-A and HADS-D were also classiﬁed as cases of comorbid anxiety-depression.

Predictor Variables Individual. Participant age at diagnosis and sex were obtained from the cancerregistries.Maritalstatus,highestlevelofeducationcompleted,employment,healthinsurancecoverage,sizeofhousehold,geographiclocation,useof complementary therapies for cancer-related purposes, and presence of physi-

cal comorbidities or signiﬁcant life events (eg, divorce) were obtained via questionnaire items at Time 1. Disease and treatment. Primary cancer type and spread of disease at diagnosis were obtained from the registries, with survivors’ cancer categorized as early/less progressed (in situ or localized; grade 1 or 2; tumor size T1 or T2), late/more progressed (invasion of adjacent organs, regional nodes or distant metastases; grade 3 or 4; not tumor size T1), or not applicable (hematologic cancers). Current remission status, cancer treatments received in the last month, and having lived away from home to receive cancer treatment were obtained via questionnaire items at Time 1. Health behaviors. Seven items adapted from existing household sur-veys assessed health behaviors. Three items assessed physical activity,23

with participants classiﬁed as sufﬁciently active (at least 150 minutes of physical activity per week), insufﬁciently active (participating in some activity but not enough in total time), or sedentary (no physical activity).24

Two items assessed smoking behavior with participants classiﬁed as current, former, or never-smokers.25 Two items assessed alcohol consumption,26 with participants who consumed more than two standard drinks on any day classiﬁed as being at increased lifetime risk of alcohol-related harm.27 These measures of physical activity and smoking have demonstrated validity and reliability compared with objective measures28 and longer self-report measures,29 respectively. Psychological. TwoitemsatTime1assessedtreatmentformentalhealth illness before and since cancer diagnosis. Coping was assessed by the 21-item Mini Mental Adjustment to Cancer (mini-MAC) scale, which measures ﬁve cancer-speciﬁc coping strategies: helplessness-hopelessness, anxious preoccupation, ﬁghting spirit, cognitive avoidance, and fatalism.30 Subscale scores were standardized from 0 to 100. Survivors who scored in the top 16% of each distribution were classiﬁed as cases on that speciﬁc coping strategy, as recommended by the mini-MAC scoring manual.31

Social. Four items at Time 1 assessed the use of community-based informationandpeersupportservicesafterdiagnosis.Perceivedsocialsupport was assessed by the Medical Outcomes Study Social Support Survey, which measures functional support: emotional/informational, tangible, affectionate, and positive social interaction.32 Subscale scores were standardized from 0 to 100. For clinical usefulness, survivors who scored in the bottom one-third of eachdistributionwereclassiﬁedashavinglowavailabilityofthatformofsocial support (C. Sherbourne, personal communication, May 2004).

Statistical Methods If one item was missing on a HADS subscale, the mean of the remaining subscale items was used.33 Data from survivors with non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma or leukemia were combined into hematologic cancer. Analysis was restricted to survivors who returned both Time 1 and Time 2 questionnaires 4 to 9 months postdiagnosis and 10 to 15 months postdiagnosis, respectively. Characteristics of Time 1 participants who did and did not complete the Time 2 questionnaire were compared using the 2 test. The point prevalence of caseness for anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety-depression was calculated for each time with 95% CIs. For each outcome, the proportions of survivorsclassiﬁedasnoncases(noncaseatTime1andTime2),resolvedcases (case at Time 1 but not at Time 2), late cases (noncase at Time 1 but case at Time 2) and chronic cases (case at Time 1 and Time 2) were calculated with 95% CIs. The association between survivors’ characteristics at Time 1 with caseness for anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety-depression at Time 2 were examined using 2 analyses (Appendix Table A1; online only). Variables with a P value .2 were included in backward stepwise logistic regression analyses. After controlling for Time 1 anxiety and depression, variables were removed if they had a P value  .1 on the likelihood ratio test; those with a P value  .05 were considered statistically signiﬁcant. Adjusted odds ratios and 95% CIs are reported for the ﬁnal models. The estimated sample size of approximately 1,320 participants would allow estimation of proportions with 95%CIswithin3%andprovide80%power,witha5%signiﬁcancelevel,to detect differences of 12% between categories of study factors predictive of anxiety and depression.

RESULTS

Sample Of 3,877 individuals assessed, 3,315 were deemed eligible and 1,691 consented to being contacted by the researchers. Overall, 1,434 survivors (43% of those deemed eligible) completed at least one of the two questionnaires: 1,360 at Time 1 and 1,270 at Time 2. Between Time 1 and Time 2, 71 participants (5%) were lost to follow-up because of death (n  34) or study withdrawal (n  37). Characteristics of the 1,154 survivors (35% of those deemed eligible) who returned both questionnaires in the speciﬁed timeframe are listed in Table 1. Although the study sample reﬂected the national proﬁle34 for the top eight incident cancers in terms of sex and age, survivors of colorectal cancer seemed to be under-represented, and hematologic and head and neck cancers seemed to be over-represented. Compared with participants who completed a Time 1 question-naireonly,thosewhocompletedbothquestionnairesweremorelikely atTime1tobeolder(25%v38%,ages60to69yearsatdiagnosis)and diagnosed with prostate cancer (14% v 28%) and were less likely to have a lung cancer diagnosis (17% v 9%) or to have anxiety (32% v 22%) or depression (27% v 12%).

Prevalence of Psychological Morbidity at 6 and 12 Months After Diagnosis Overall, the point prevalence of caseness for each outcome was low, and was similar for Time 1 and Time 2 (Table 2). Of the three outcomes, anxiety was the most common with a prevalence of 22% at Time 1 (95% CI, 20% to 25%) and 21% at Time 2 (95% CI, 19% to 24%). At both Time 1 and Time 2, 13% of survivors (95% CI, 11% to 14%) were identiﬁed as cases of depression and 9% (95% CI, 7% to 10%) were identiﬁed as cases of comorbid anxiety-depression.

Prevalence of Course of Psychological Morbidity Figure1showstheproportionofsurvivorswhowerecategorized tothefourpathwaysnoncase,chroniccase,latecase,andresolvedcase for each outcome. The most prevalent pathway was noncase for anxiety (70%; 95% CI, 68% to 73%), depression (82%; 95% CI, 79% to 84%),andcomorbidanxiety-depression(87%;95%CI,85%to89%). The prevalence of the chronic case pathway was low and was more prevalent for anxiety (14%; 95% CI, 12% to 16%) than depression (6%; 95% CI, 5% to 8%) or comorbid anxiety-depression (4%; 95% CI, 3% to 5%). The occurrence of the late case pathway was also low for anxiety (7%; 95% CI, 6% to 9%), depression (6%; 95% CI, 5% to 8%), and comorbid anxiety-depression (5%; 95% CI, 3% to 6%). A similarly small proportion of survivors who were cases at Time 1 recovered to noncase levels of anxiety (8%; 95% CI, 7% to 10%), depression (6%; 95% CI, 5% to 8%), and comorbid anxiety-depression (4%; 95% CI, 3% to 5%) by Time 2.

Time 1 Predictors of Chronic or Late Psychological Morbidity at Time 2 The Time 1 characteristics that predicted caseness for anxiety, depression, and comorbid anxiety-depression at Time 2 are listed in Table 3, Table 4, and Table 5. Female participants (odds ratio [OR], 1.8) had almost twice the odds of being a case of anxiety than male participants. Similarly, survivors who were cases of depression at Time 1 had higher odds of being cases of anxiety (OR, 1.9), depression (OR, 6.9), and comorbid anxiety-depression (OR, 6.3) than those who were noncases of depression at Time 1. Survivors who used cognitive avoidance coping had greater odds of being cases of depression (OR, 1.7) and comorbid anxiety-depression (OR, 1.8) whereas those who used ﬁghting spirit had higher odds (OR, 1.7) of being cases of anxiety compared with those who didn’t use these strategies.

DISCUSSION

This large-scale longitudinal study found that the point preva-lenceofanxiety,depression,andcomorbidanxiety-depressionamong cancer survivors did not decrease over time. At both times, approximately 20% of survivors were cases of anxiety, 13% were cases of depression,and9%werecasesofcomorbidanxiety-depression.Analysis of the course of anxiety and depression revealed a large group of survivors who demonstrated a pattern of psychological functioning consistent with resilience. Small groups of survivors experienced trajectories indicative of recovered, chronic, and late psychological morbidity. Compared with simple point prevalence data for each time, these four clinically important patterns of adjustment provide a more complete picture of the psychological wellbeing of cancer survivors during early survivorship. The ﬁnding that most survivors were not cases of anxiety and/or depression at either time point is consistent with previous studies conducted of survivors of breast,5,8,9 colorectal,7 lung,6 and head and

Given that feelings of vulnerability are common when active treatment is completed,35 it may be reassuring to give survivors in late treatment the message that most will adjust well and require only low-intensity supportive care, including information and self-management support.2,36

To our knowledge, no other studies of the psychological outcomes of survivors in early survivorship have examined the relative contribution of the array of factors considered in our study. Poten-tially modiﬁable factors were the strongest and most consistent predictors of late or chronic anxiety and/or depression. Consistentwithpreviousﬁndings,6,7,37casenessatTime1wasthe strongest predictor of caseness at Time 2. Smoking status (current or former)andphysicalactivity(insufﬁcientlyactive)atTime1uniquely predicted caseness for comorbid anxiety-depression and depression, respectively, at Time 2. This is consistent with evidence that physical activity might have beneﬁcial effects on psychological well-being.38

Coping strategies at Time 1 also predicted caseness for psychological morbidity at Time 2, albeit to a lesser extent. Treatments received in the month before Time 1 assessment did not signiﬁcantly predict psychological morbidity at Time 2.

Cancer type uniquely predicted caseness for depression, with onlysurvivorsoflungcancermorelikelytobecasesatTime2,possibly reﬂecting the poor prognosis associated with this cancer type. This is a uniquecontributionas,toourknowledge,nootherstudyhasincluded a diversity of cancer types with sufﬁcient numbers to conduct ade-quately powered subgroup analyses. Though previous ﬁndings are mixed, our study found that female sex predicted caseness for anxiety and not being in remission predicted caseness for depression. These ﬁndings may suggest that routine psychological screening of all cancer survivors during survivorship is not warranted. Rather, screening during survivorship may best be targeted at survivors at greatestriskofpersistentorlatepsychologicalmorbidity,thatis,those who screen as cases of psychological morbidity at the end of active treatment, were diagnosed with lung cancer, are former or current smokers, or are insufﬁciently active. Though the detection of cases of psychological morbidity requires screening tools with a high degree of accuracy, information about cancer type and health risk behaviors is readilyavailableintheclinicalsetting,makingthisgroupofvulnerable

This is one of the ﬁrst studies to examine the prevalence and predictors of the short-term courses of anxiety and/or depression among a diverse sample of cancer survivors in early survivorship. Although a population-based sampling frame was used, the 43% response rate may raise concerns about response bias. However, sample retention between Time 1 and Time 2 was high (95%). Analysis was restricted to survivors who returned both questionnaires, and because attrition from Time 1 to Time 2 was not completely random, the results may slightly underestimate psychological morbidity. Though assessments were anchored to clearly deﬁned time points postdiagnosis, there is much heterogeneity in the timing of transition from treatment to survivorship. Ideally, assessment points should be linked to key clinical events (eg, end of hospital-based treatment), in line with the approach described by Helselmans et al.5 Furthermore, the registry-based recruitment method did not allow assessment of psychological morbidity around the time of diagnosis. In balancing thesurveylengthandbreadth,itwasnotpossibletoassessallpotential risk factors (eg, diet). As it was not feasible to assess psychological morbidityusingagoldstandardstructuredclinicalinterviewgiventhe large and dispersed sample, we used the HADS. Although recent reviews have recommended the HADS as the tool of choice in oncology populations,39,40 screening tools are not diagnostic, have a ten-dency to overestimate cases, and may not detect cancer-speciﬁc distress such as fear of recurrence. Inconclusion,between6and12monthspostdiagnosis,themajority ofcancersurvivorsdemonstratedatrajectoryofpsychologicaladjustment indicative of resilience or recovery.
